Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
ruminate about how event could have been prevented
avoid anything that could be stressful

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

issues.explanation: These items form a combat/interpersonal-violence style hypervigilance pattern centered on armed human threat, which is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma. A disaster survivor may be generally vigilant, but carrying a weapon and scanning for weapons specifically are not a coherent extension of the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: The threat profile is narrowly organized around deliberate human attack (weapons, tactical positioning), while the memory items are generic intrusion/detachment phenomena and do not support that specific threat theme. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a plausible disaster-related PTSD presentation.

vignette: Henry had always been a man who took pride in his ability to stay calm under pressure. As a tutor, he was accustomed to helping students navigate challenging material and managing his own stress levels with ease. But all of that changed when the Category 5 hurricane tore through his coastal town two years ago. The storm had been predicted to make landfall hours later than it did, leaving Henry and his wife scrambling to secure their home and flee to safety. The howling winds and lashing rain created a maelstrom that seemed to go on forever, and when the waters finally receded, Henry's neighborhood was left in ruins. At first, Henry tried to tackle the cleanup efforts head-on, but as he worked through the wreckage of his home, memories of that terrifying night began to flood back. He would recall the sound of the wind screaming like a banshee outside, and then suddenly feel completely numb, as if it had all happened to someone else. Other times, the smell of saltwater and mud would transport him back to that desperate, clinging-to-life moment when the storm surge threatened to engulf their home. As the memories resurfaced, Henry found himself ruminating on how they could have prevented the damage – if only they'd boarded up the windows sooner, or evacuated earlier. He'd spend hours going over every decision, wondering what he could've done differently. It was as if by replaying that fateful night in his mind, he could somehow prevent it from happening again. But this constant dwelling on what might have been took a toll. Henry started to feel like the universe was conspiring against him – when something took longer than expected, he'd assume the worst, convinced that disaster lurked just around the corner. He'd scan every room he entered for potential dangers, positioning himself with his back against a wall so he could keep an eye out for any signs of trouble. As time went on, Henry's fixation on safety began to affect his daily life as a tutor. He started avoiding teaching sessions that might take place in unfamiliar locations or at odd hours – the uncertainty was just too much to handle. His wife grew concerned about the changes she saw in him, but Henry reassured her that he just needed some more time to process what had happened. Yet even with all his efforts to avoid stressors, the memories continued to force their way into his mind, often at the most inopportune moments – during sessions with students, or while trying to relax at home. When this happened, Henry would dissociate from the recollections, pretending they'd happened to someone else – it was the only way he knew how to cope. The loop of memories, ruminations, and fears began to tighten its grip on Henry's life. He became increasingly withdrawn, struggling to connect with his students or enjoy time with his wife. It wasn't until a particularly difficult session with a student – one where Henry had dissociated so completely that he barely remembered what they'd discussed – that he realized something was very wrong. Henry confided in his wife about how overwhelmed he felt, and together they decided it was time to seek help. As he sat in the therapist's office for their first appointment, Henry couldn't shake the feeling of being trapped, with the weight of those memories pressing down on him like a physical force. He knew that breaking free from this cycle would be no easy task – but for the sake of his relationships and his own sanity, he was willing to try.
